Upon successfully completing this course, students will be able to:

Knowledge
  • Clarify the definitions of “culture” and “popular culture”
  • Explain Bourdieu’s theorization of “aristocracy of culture”; “cultural capital”; “symbolic power”; “symbolic good”
  • Explain critical terms such as self-branding, visibility, affective economy, parasocial relationships, gamification

Skill
  • Identify the power dynamics that underlie different cultural constructs such as majority and minority cultures; subcultures and countercultures in the social context that the students are familiar with.
  • Apply the theoretical concepts of fan practices in the analysis of popular culture content
  • Analyze celebrity figures from economic, cultural, social, political and technological perspectives of celebrity culture

 Character
  • Critically evaluate the social outcome of gamification
  • Critically evaluate the outcome of the celebritization of the public sphere and everyday life

If acquiring popularity is a good thing, why do we also strive for niche and non-mainstream tastes? Can anyone, any type of cultural activity become popular? How is popularity conceptualized and manufactured in the entertainment industry and by digital platforms? If a star is popular in one cultural context, does this ensure one’s popularity in another culture?

Revolving around the concept of being “popular”, this course introduces students to several foundational cultural theories and invites them to analyze contemporary cultural practices where digital technologies infiltrate every aspect of our lives. The course starts with academic discussions on popular culture, cultural capital, language and symbolic power. This is to argue that cultural practices are socially marked and also used by people to market their social identities. Then we zoom into different industries to see how celebrity is manufactured, how fandom activities developed and how digital platforms demand our attention. We also reflect on the “unpopular” things and cultural practices that intend to hide from the public. This helps us to understand cultural practices in relation to social norms and power.

In the classroom, we will meet students from different programs such as online culture, sociology, communication, and social psychology. The course tries to invite students to bring knowledge from their programs to form interdisciplinary talks.
The material of this course is composed of selected articles and book chapters. Detailed information will be announced on Canvas in accordance with the course syllabus.
